Mission 1

Mission 1: Why do some churches share bread every day and others only once a month?

Make a guess: Why do some churches share bread every day and others only once a month?

Mission 1Read the source

Luke's Last Supper

> "He received a cup, and when he had given thanks, he said, "Take this and share it amongst yourselves, for I tell you, I will not drink at all again from the fruit of the vine, until God's Kingdom comes."" (Luke 22:17–18, WEBBE)

> "He took bread, and when he had given thanks, he broke and gave it to them, saying, "This is my body which is given for you. Do this in memory of me."" (Luke 22:19, WEBBE)

> "Likewise, he took the cup after supper, saying, "This cup is the new covenant in my blood, which is poured out for you."" (Luke 22:20, WEBBE)

  • Setting: a Passover meal (Luke 22:15), remembering Israel's rescue from Egypt.
  • Luke alone has two cups: one before the bread (17), one "after supper" (20).

Q1 What does Jesus tell the disciples to do?

Show answer

Take, share, and repeat the bread action "in memory of me".

Q2 Which phrase looks to the future?

Show answer

"Until God's Kingdom comes": the meal anticipates the Kingdom.

Mission 1

What did Jesus' actions mean?

  • New covenant: Jesus' death begins the promised new relationship between God and his people (Jeremiah 31:31).
  • Sacrifice: "given for you", "poured out for you": his death is an offering for others.
  • Command: "Do this": the Church must keep repeating the meal.
  • Remembrance (anamnesis): for Catholics and Orthodox, not just recalling but making the saving event present; for Baptists, a recalling and proclaiming of Christ's death.
  • Kingdom: each celebration looks ahead to the feast of God's Kingdom.
  • Catholic reading: Jesus instituted the Mass and the priesthood; the Mass makes present the one sacrifice of the cross (it does not repeat it).
  • Baptist reading: Jesus gave an ordinance to remember his death "until he comes" (1 Corinthians 11:26); the cross was once for all, so the Supper offers no sacrifice.
Mission 1

The Catholic Mass

  • Celebrated daily; Catholics must attend on Sundays and holy days of obligation.
  • Liturgy of the Word (readings, homily), then Liturgy of the Eucharist.
  • Only an ordained priest may consecrate, using the words of institution at the altar.
  • Unleavened hosts; the cup is sometimes offered to the people too.
  • Receivers fast for one hour and should not be conscious of serious (mortal) sin; First Holy Communion at about age 7–8.
  • Remaining hosts are kept in the tabernacle; the red sanctuary lamp shows Christ present.
  • Importance: the "source and summit" of the Christian life (Second Vatican Council, Lumen Gentium 11, 1964).
Mission 1

The Baptist Lord's Supper

  • Held weekly in some churches, monthly in many; often after the sermon.
  • Led by the minister, or by elders or deacons: there is no priest; all believers are priests (1 Peter 2:9).
  • A communion table, not an altar: a meal, not a sacrifice.
  • The leader reads Jesus' words at the Last Supper (often 1 Corinthians 11:23–26).
  • Bread (sometimes an ordinary loaf) and small individual cups of wine or, often, non-alcoholic grape juice, passed to people in their seats.
  • Often everyone eats and drinks together, to show unity.
  • Usually an open table: all who love and trust Christ may share, whatever their church.
  • Importance: obedience to Christ's command, remembrance, fellowship. Less frequent sharing is meant to keep it special, not to make it unimportant.
Quick check
?Which practice is shared by both Catholic and Baptist celebrations?
Mission 1Evaluate

Does belief shape practice more than anything else?

  • Claim: Differences in Eucharistic practice are caused mainly by differences in belief.
  • For: belief in Christ's lasting presence → tabernacle, adoration, reverence for crumbs; belief in a memorial → table, open sharing.
  • For: a sacrificial view needs a priest and altar; a meal view needs neither.
  • Against: history and culture matter too: e.g. individual cups and grape juice spread with 19th-century hygiene and temperance movements, not new doctrine.
  • Against: churches with similar beliefs (e.g. different Anglican parishes) still practise very differently.
  • Judgement criteria: Can each practice be traced to a belief? What else (history, culture, authority) explains it?
Mission check

?A Catholic and her Baptist friend attend each other's churches. Each is surprised. Which pair of surprises best fits the two traditions?

The same words, "Do this", lead to different practices because of what each tradition believes is happening.

Mission 2

Mission 2: A bishop chained between soldiers begs his friends not to save him. What was he writing, and why?

Make a guess: A bishop chained between soldiers begs his friends not to save him. What was he writing, and why?

Mission 2

The Apostolic Fathers

  • A modern label (from the 17th century) for the earliest Christian writers after the New Testament, about AD 90–150, thought to have known the apostles or their followers.
  • Usually included: 1 Clement (Rome to Corinth, about 96); Ignatius' seven letters; Polycarp, To the Philippians; the Didache; the Epistle of Barnabas; the Shepherd of Hermas; the Martyrdom of Polycarp; 2 Clement; fragments of Papias; (often) the Epistle to Diognetus.
  • Concerns: church order and leadership; holiness; false teaching; persecution; Christianity's relation to Judaism.
  • Not apologists: they write mainly to churches, not to outsiders (contrast Justin, written to the emperor).
  • Value: a bridge between the apostles and the later Church; evidence for early worship and ministry.
Mission 2

Ignatius and his journey

  • Bishop of Antioch in Syria, where "the disciples were first called Christians" (Acts 11:26); Eusebius lists him as the second or third bishop after Peter.
  • Arrested in Antioch; taken under guard to Rome to die in the arena, under Trajan (Eusebius dates it about 107–108; many say 110–117; a minority later).
  • Guarded by ten soldiers, whom he calls "leopards" who grow worse when treated kindly (To the Romans 5, paraphrase).
  • Route across Asia Minor. At Smyrna he meets Polycarp and envoys from Ephesus, Magnesia and Tralles; at Troas he hears that peace has returned to the church in Antioch.
  • Taken on through Macedonia (Philippi; Polycarp's letter, 9, remembers him); died in Rome; later tradition places his death in the Colosseum.
Mission 2

The seven letters

  • From Smyrna: Ephesians, Magnesians, Trallians (to churches whose bishops had visited him) and Romans (asking them not to intervene).
  • From Troas: Philadelphians, Smyrnaeans and a personal letter To Polycarp.
  • Written quickly, in vivid, compressed Greek, by a prisoner facing death.
  • Recensions: a short Syriac version (published 1845), a long version with later additions and extra letters (4th century), and the middle recension of seven letters, defended by Theodor Zahn (1873) and J. B. Lightfoot (1828–1889), The Apostolic Fathers, Part II (1885). The middle recension is now accepted by most scholars.
  • A minority (e.g. Robert Joly, 1979) argue the letters are later forgeries.
Mission 2

Unity and obedience to the bishop

  • Ignatius is the first to describe a threefold ministry in each church: one bishop (episkopos), a council of presbyters (elders), and deacons.
  • The bishop presides in the place of God; presbyters as the council of the apostles; deacons entrusted with the service of Jesus Christ (Magnesians 6, paraphrase).
  • Do nothing without the bishop (Trallians 2; Smyrnaeans 8, paraphrase).
  • One Eucharist, one flesh of Christ, one cup, one altar, one bishop (Philadelphians 4, paraphrase).
  • Only a Eucharist under the bishop, or one he authorises, is valid. "Wherever the bishop appears, there let the people be; just as wherever Jesus Christ is, there is the catholic Church" (Smyrnaeans 8, paraphrase): the first surviving use of "catholic" (universal) for the Church.
  • Purpose: unity in the face of division and false teaching; obedience to the bishop is obedience to God.
Quick check
?According to Ignatius, how should the presbyters of a local church be understood?
Mission 2

Heresy: docetism

  • Docetists (from Greek dokein, "to seem"): Christ only seemed to have a body and to suffer.
  • Ignatius' answer: Jesus was truly born of Mary, truly ate and drank, was truly crucified under Pontius Pilate, truly raised (Trallians 9, paraphrase; Smyrnaeans 1–3).
  • If Christ only seemed to suffer, then Ignatius' chains and coming death are pointless (Trallians 10, paraphrase).
  • Docetists stay away from the Eucharist because they do not confess it to be the flesh of our Saviour who suffered (Smyrnaeans 7, paraphrase).
  • The Eucharist is "the medicine of immortality" (Ephesians 20, short phrase).
  • Defence: stay with the bishop; avoid the false teachers "like wild beasts" (Ephesians 7, paraphrase).
Mission 2

Judaisers

  • Judaisers: Christians (or teachers) who urged Jewish practices, such as Sabbath observance, or explained Christ only through Jewish law.
  • "It is absurd to speak of Jesus Christ and to judaise" (Magnesians 10, paraphrase): Christianity did not believe in Judaism, but Judaism in Christianity.
  • Those who once lived by the old ways now live "no longer keeping the Sabbath but the Lord's Day" (Magnesians 9, paraphrase).
  • The prophets themselves looked forward to Christ (Magnesians 8; Philadelphians 5).
  • At Philadelphia some said: "If I do not find it in the archives (the scriptures), I do not believe it in the gospel." Ignatius: "my archives are Jesus Christ", his cross, death and resurrection (Philadelphians 8, paraphrase).
  • Scholars debate whether Ignatius faced two groups (docetists and Judaisers) or one mixed group.
  • Note: this is an intra-Christian debate about identity; it has also fed later Christian hostility to Judaism, which most churches now reject.
Mission 2Read the source

The glory of martyrdom (To the Romans)

Paraphrase of To the Romans 4–6:

  • He writes to all the churches that he dies willingly for God, unless they hinder him.
  • He begs: do not show him an "untimely kindness". "Let me be food for the wild beasts."
  • "I am the wheat of God, ground by the teeth of the beasts, that I may be found pure bread of Christ" (short phrase from Romans 4; paraphrase of the rest).
  • Only now is he beginning to be a disciple.
  • "Allow me to be an imitator of the passion of my God" (Romans 6, paraphrase).

Q1 What image does Ignatius use for himself, and why might it suit a Eucharistic theology?

Show answer

Wheat ground into bread: his death becomes an offering, like the Eucharistic bread.

Q2 Why does he plead with the Romans?

Show answer

He fears they will use influence to save him and so prevent his martyrdom.

Quick check
?Ignatius writes that docetists stay away from the Eucharist. Why does he connect their heresy with this?
Mission 2Evaluate

Did Ignatius describe church order or create it?

  • Describing: he writes as if one bishop already leads in Ephesus, Magnesia, Tralles, Philadelphia and Smyrna, and names them (e.g. Onesimus, Damas, Polybius).
  • Describing: the Pastoral Epistles already speak of bishops and deacons (1 Timothy 3).
  • Creating or promoting: his insistence suggests the pattern was new or resisted; in the NT "bishop" and "presbyter" overlap (Titus 1:5–7); To the Romans names no bishop in Rome, and 1 Clement shows collective leadership there.
  • Creating or promoting: a prisoner with no authority outside Antioch is arguing a case, not reporting a settled fact.
  • Significance: Catholic, Orthodox and Anglican churches see in him early evidence for the historic episcopate (bishops in succession from the apostles); many Protestant historians see a development beyond the NT.
  • Judge it by: Is a letter good evidence of what was normal? Does development mean departure, or faithful growth?
Mission 2Evaluate

Was Ignatius' desire for martyrdom healthy?

  • Concern: he seems to seek death; some modern readers call his language morbid, even close to suicide.
  • Concern: the Martyrdom of Polycarp (4) later warns against volunteering for martyrdom.
  • Defence: he did not choose arrest: he accepts a sentence already given and refuses rescue.
  • Defence: his aim is imitation of Christ's passion and true discipleship; his words are rhetorical and shaped by intense faith, not a death wish.
  • Defence: his martyrdom served the unity of the churches, strengthening their witness.
  • Judge it by: Is there a difference between accepting death and desiring it? How should a modern reader judge a letter by a man facing execution?
Mission 2

Pastoral and theological issues for leaders

  • From Ignatius' letters, the issues every religious leader faces:
  • Unity: holding a community together across disagreement.
  • Authority: how much obedience a leader can ask, and on what basis.
  • Truth: guarding teaching against error (docetism) without harshness.
  • Identity: relating to a parent tradition (Judaism) and to the wider culture.
  • Suffering: supporting believers under pressure, and facing it personally.
  • Care: To Polycarp gives advice: bear with all, care for widows and slaves, "stand firm like an anvil being struck" (paraphrase, 3).
Mission 2Evaluate

Are Ignatius' concerns still relevant for religious leaders?

  • For: churches still face division; Ignatius' call to unity around shared worship (one Eucharist) inspires ecumenical work.
  • For: leaders still must address teaching that denies core beliefs (e.g. the full humanity of Christ).
  • For: many leaders today, in countries where believers are persecuted, face pressures close to his.
  • Against: strong stress on obedience to one leader can enable abuse of power; safeguarding failures in many churches show the danger.
  • Against: many churches (Congregational, Baptist, Quaker and many Pentecostal) practise shared or congregational leadership and have no monarchical bishop.
  • Judge it by: Is the bishop's authority tied to unity and service, or to control? Does Ignatius' model fit communities that are not under persecution?
Mission check

?A modern religious community splits: one group meets separately and celebrates its own services, saying its own leaders are holier than the appointed leader. A senior figure writes to both: "Have one service, around one leader, so that you remain one body." Which theme of Ignatius' letters does this letter most closely echo?

Unity, truth and faithful witness: a condemned bishop's letters became an early blueprint for church leadership, and are still argued over.

Mission 3

Mission 3: Christians were called atheists and cannibals. How did a philosopher in a cloak answer the emperor?

Make a guess: Christians were called atheists and cannibals. How did a philosopher in a cloak answer the emperor?

Mission 3

Why "apologists"?

  • Apology (Greek apologia): a reasoned defence, as in a law court. Not saying sorry.
  • "Always be ready to give an answer to everyone who asks you a reason concerning the hope that is in you" (1 Peter 3:15, WEBBE). The Greek for "answer" is apologia.
  • In the 2nd century Christianity was illegal in practice: being a Christian could bring death, often after a private accusation.
  • Popular rumours (listed by Athenagoras, Plea 3, c. 177):
  • Atheism: Christians refused the gods and the emperor cult.
  • "Thyestean feasts": cannibalism (a garbled report of eating the "body and blood").
  • "Oedipodean intercourse": incest (Christians called each other "brother" and "sister" and met in private).
  • The apologists wrote to answer these charges and to win a fair hearing.
Mission 3

The apologists

  • Greek apologists, mostly addressed to emperors or educated pagans:
  • Quadratus and Aristides (to Hadrian, c. 125; Aristides' addressee is disputed).
  • Justin Martyr (c. 100–c. 165): the fullest surviving early apologist.
  • Tatian (Justin's pupil), Address to the Greeks (c. 170s): hostile to Greek culture.
  • Athenagoras, A Plea for the Christians (c. 177, to Marcus Aurelius and Commodus).
  • Theophilus of Antioch, To Autolycus (c. 180): first known use of Trias (triad) for God.
  • Later, in Latin: Tertullian, Apology (197), and Minucius Felix, Octavius.
  • Two attitudes to pagan learning: bridge (Justin, Athenagoras) or wall (Tatian; often Tertullian).
Mission 3

Justin's life

  • Born c. 100 at Flavia Neapolis (modern Nablus) in Samaria, to a Gentile family.
  • A seeker: tried Stoic, Peripatetic (Aristotelian) and Pythagorean teachers, then loved Platonism (Dialogue 2).
  • By the sea he met an old man who pointed him to the Hebrew prophets and to Christ (Dialogue 3–8). Converted c. 130.
  • He was also struck by the courage of Christians facing death (Second Apology 12).
  • Kept the philosopher's cloak; taught Christianity as the true philosophy, in a school in Rome.
  • Accused (he suspected the Cynic Crescens, Second Apology 3), tried before the prefect Junius Rusticus, beheaded with six companions, c. 165 (Acts of Justin). Hence "Martyr".
Mission 3

Three writings

  • First Apology (c. 150–155): to Emperor Antoninus Pius and his adopted sons (one is the future Marcus Aurelius), the Senate and people of Rome. The main defence; ends with a description of baptism and Sunday worship (61–67; –b).
  • Second Apology (c. 155–161): shorter, possibly an appendix to the first. Prompted by an injustice in Rome: Ptolemaeus and Lucius executed simply for confessing the name "Christian" (Second Apology 2).
  • Dialogue with Trypho the Jew (c. 155–160): a debate with Trypho, a Jew who fled the recent war in Judea (the Bar Kokhba revolt, 132–135), set (says Eusebius) at Ephesus. Addressed to Jews and to Christians, not to Rome.
Mission 3

Political arguments

  • Justice: Rome punishes Christians for a name, not for crimes. "From a name neither praise nor punishment could reasonably spring" (First Apology 4, ANF translation). Investigate first; punish only proven crimes (First Apology 2–3).
  • Loyalty: Christians pay their taxes, as Jesus taught ("Give to Caesar the things that are Caesar's", Mark 12:17), and they pray for the rulers (First Apology 17).
  • No rival kingdom: the kingdom Christians await is not a human one (First Apology 11). If it were, they would hide their faith to survive.
  • Good citizens: people who believe God sees every deed make the best subjects (First Apology 12).
  • A warning: rulers who choose injustice will face God's judgement (First Apology 68).
Mission 3

Moral arguments

  • Not atheists: Christians reject the gods of myth, but worship "the most true God" (First Apology 6, paraphrase).
  • Changed lives: those who once loved sexual vice, magic, money and hatred now live chastely, share their goods and pray for their enemies (First Apology 14).
  • Higher morals than their accusers: Christians do not expose (abandon) unwanted babies (First Apology 27, 29).
  • Rumours rejected: no secret cannibal or incestuous rites; Justin describes the real Sunday meeting openly (First Apology 65–67).
  • Courage: Christians die rather than deny Christ, which liars and criminals would not do (Second Apology 12).
Mission 3Read the source

Christ and the philosophers

Justin, First Apology 46 (ANF translation, 1885):

> "those who lived reasonably are Christians, even though they have been thought atheists"

His examples are Socrates and Heraclitus among the Greeks. And in Second Apology 13:

> "Whatever things were rightly said among all men, are the property of us Christians."

  • "Reasonably" translates meta logou: "with the Logos" (Word, Reason).

Q1 Why could Justin call Socrates a Christian?

Show answer

He lived by the Logos, whom Justin identifies with Christ.

Q2 Which pagan charge does the first quotation turn back on the accusers?

Show answer

Atheism: Socrates too was condemned as an atheist.

Mission 3

Philosophical arguments

  • Logos (Word, Reason): in Stoic and Platonic thought, the rational order of the world. John 1:1 calls Christ "the Word".
  • Logos spermatikos (the "seed-bearing" or "seminal" Word): a seed of the Logos is sown in every human mind (Second Apology 8, 13). So philosophers saw part of the truth.
  • In Christ the whole Logos became human. So Christianity is the true philosophy: it completes what Greek thought began.
  • Plato borrowed from Moses: Justin claims Plato's ideas on creation and free will came from the Hebrew scriptures (First Apology 44, 59). Few historians accept this.
  • Demons imitated Christian truths in myths and stirred up persecution, as they did against Socrates (First Apology 5, 54).
Mission 3

Theological arguments

  • God: one, eternal, unbegotten, beyond name; Father and Creator.
  • Christ: the Logos, God's Son, born as man, crucified, risen. Worshipped "in the second place", the prophetic Spirit in the third (First Apology 13): an early, not yet worked-out, pattern of Trinity.
  • Proof from prophecy: the Hebrew prophets foretold Christ's birth, life, death and the spread of the church long before (First Apology 30–53). Fulfilled prophecy shows divine truth, not magic.
  • Judgement and resurrection: God will raise the dead and judge; so Christians do not fear death.
  • Worship: baptism and the Eucharist explained, to show there is nothing shameful (First Apology 61–67).
Quick check
?Justin calls Socrates a Christian "before Christ". Which idea makes this possible for him?
Mission 3

Dialogue with Trypho

  • The Law: the Mosaic laws (circumcision, Sabbath, food laws) were temporary, given because of Israel's hardness of heart; Christ brings a new covenant (Dialogue 11–12, 18).
  • The true Israel: Christians, Jewish and Gentile, are "the true spiritual Israel" (Dialogue 11).
  • Jesus the Messiah: proved from the scriptures Trypho accepts. Isaiah 7:14: "the virgin will conceive" (WEBBE). Trypho replies that the text should read "young woman" (Dialogue 43, 67).
  • The Logos in the Old Testament: the one who appeared to Abraham at Mamre and to Moses was God's Word, "another" divine Lord distinct from the Father in number, not in will (Dialogue 56, paraphrase).
  • Polite in tone, but it set a supersessionist pattern (the church replacing Israel) that later fed Christian hostility to Jews.
Quick check
?How does the Dialogue with Trypho differ from the two Apologies?
Mission 3Evaluate

How successful was Justin's defence?

  • Claim: Justin's apologetic was effective.
  • For: He gave Christianity intellectual credibility: a faith educated Romans could discuss.
  • For: His Logos theology shaped later thought (Irenaeus, Clement of Alexandria, Origen); his account of worship is invaluable evidence.
  • For: He answered each slander with specific evidence, not just denial.
  • Against: No sign the emperors read or answered it; persecution continued, and Justin himself was executed.
  • Against: Weak arguments by modern standards: Plato borrowing from Moses; demons as explanation; reading prophecy selectively.
  • Against: The bridge to philosophy risks diluting the gospel (Tatian's and Tertullian's worry); the Dialogue's view of Judaism is now widely criticised.
  • Judgement criteria: Effective for whom (emperors, educated pagans, Christians)? In his time or long-term? Measured by persuasion or by survival of the faith?
Mission 3Evaluate

Writers who defend faith in any age

  • Claim: Apologetics strengthens faith more than it converts outsiders.
  • For: Most readers of apologetics are believers; it gives them confidence to stay and speak (as 1 Peter 3:15 asks).
  • For: Faith is often said to rest on experience, community or grace, not on argument.
  • Against: Apologists do help some outsiders: Justin's Dialogue is itself a conversion story driven by argument; C. S. Lewis is often cited by adult converts.
  • Against: Apologetics also shapes public respect: a faith that can give reasons wins a hearing (Justin; Alister McGrath's replies to the "new atheists").
  • Risk: apologists answer the questions of their own culture; arguments date (Justin's Plato-borrowed-from-Moses claim).
  • Judgement criteria: Who is the audience? Is the aim proof, plausibility or respect? Does it change minds, or behaviour (like the changed lives Justin points to)?
Mission check

?A modern Christian writer argues: "The scientific search for order in nature is itself a clue: whatever is true in science belongs to the God who made a rational world." Which of Justin's arguments does this most closely echo?

Justin's bridge between faith and reason is still used by apologists today. Next: Constantine, when the emperor himself took the Christian side.

Mission 4

Mission 4: An emperor put a Christian sign on his soldiers' shields. Was it faith, politics, or both?

Make a guess: An emperor put a Christian sign on his soldiers' shields. Was it faith, politics, or both?

Mission 4

The world Constantine was born into

  • Late 3rd century: the empire had survived decades of civil war, invasion and crisis.
  • Diocletian (emperor 284–305) set up the Tetrarchy (rule of four, 293): two senior emperors (Augusti) and two juniors (Caesars).
  • The Great Persecution began in 303 under Diocletian and Galerius: churches destroyed, scriptures burned, clergy arrested, sacrifice enforced.
  • Traditional religion was bound up with loyalty: the gods protected the state, so refusing them looked like treason.
Mission 4

Family and early career

  • Born c. 272–273 at Naissus (Niš, in modern Serbia).
  • Father: Constantius Chlorus, Caesar in the West from 293, Augustus from 305. Mother: Helena, later a devoted Christian (her pilgrimage to the Holy Land, c. 326–328).
  • Constantine grew up at Diocletian's court in Nicomedia: a soldier and, in effect, a hostage for his father's loyalty.
  • Constantius was the tetrarch least keen on persecution: in his lands, according to Lactantius, he only pulled down church buildings.
  • 305: Diocletian retired. Constantine was passed over for Caesar; he escaped to join his father and crossed with him to Britain.
Mission 4

The struggle for the West, 306–313

  • 25 July 306: Constantius died at York; his troops acclaimed Constantine emperor. Galerius grudgingly recognised him as Caesar.
  • Oct 306: Maxentius (son of the retired Maximian) seized Rome and Italy.
  • 310: Maximian plotted against Constantine and died. Constantine now claimed descent from the emperor Claudius Gothicus; a panegyric (praise-speech) of 310 says he saw a vision of Apollo at a temple in Gaul.
  • 311: dying, Galerius issued an edict of toleration for Christians.
  • 312: Constantine invaded Italy, won at Turin and Verona, and on 28 October 312 defeated Maxentius at the Milvian Bridge outside Rome. Maxentius drowned in the Tiber.
  • 313: at Milan, Constantine and Licinius (emperor in the East) agreed religious freedom for all and the return of Christian property.
Mission 4Read the source

Lactantius

Lactantius (c. 250–c. 325), a Christian rhetorician, later tutor to Constantine's son Crispus. On the Deaths of the Persecutors 44 (written c. 314–315; ANF translation, 1886):

> "Constantine was directed in a dream to cause the heavenly sign to be delineated on the shields of his soldiers"

  • The sign: the letter Χ with a line drawn through it, "turned round thus at the top, being the cipher of Christ". Either the Chi-Rho (☧) or a staurogram (a cross with a loop at the top); scholars disagree.
  • When: the night before the battle. No vision in the sky.

Q1 How did Constantine receive the instruction?

Show answer

In a dream.

Q2 Why is Lactantius' account valuable?

Show answer

Written within about three years of the battle by a Christian close to the court.

Mission 4Read the source

Eusebius

Eusebius of Caesarea (c. 260–339), bishop and church historian. Life of Constantine 1.28–29 (written c. 337–339, after Constantine's death; NPNF translation, 1890):

  • At midday, on campaign (time and place not given), Constantine "saw with his own eyes the trophy of a cross of light in the heavens, above the sun", with the words "Conquer by this" (Greek touto nika; Latin in hoc signo vinces).
  • His whole army saw it too.
  • That night Christ appeared to him in his sleep with the same sign and told him to make a likeness of it as a safeguard in battle: the labarum (a Chi-Rho standard).
  • Eusebius says Constantine told him this himself, years later, and "confirmed his statement by an oath".

Q1 What does Eusebius add that Lactantius lacks?

Show answer

A daytime vision in the sky, seen by the army; the words; the labarum.

Q2 Why might that matter?

Show answer

The story grew, or Eusebius had new information from the emperor.

Mission 4

Comparing the accounts

  • Agree: a divine sign; Christ's monogram or cross; used in battle; victory credited to the Christian God.
  • Differ:
  • Date written: Lactantius c. 314–315; Eusebius 25 years later.
  • Form: dream only (Lactantius); sky vision and dream (Eusebius).
  • Witnesses: Constantine alone (Lactantius); the whole army (Eusebius).
  • Silence: Eusebius' own Church History (9.9, c. 315) tells of the battle and Constantine's prayer, but no vision.
  • Possible explanations: legend growing; Constantine's own memory shaping the story; a natural event. One theory (Peter Weiss, 1993) links it to a solar halo seen in 310 and later understood as Christian.
Quick check
?Which statement about the two accounts of Constantine's conversion is accurate?
Mission 4

Signs of an older faith

  • Arch of Constantine (dedicated 315, by the Senate): victory "by the prompting of the divinity" (instinctu divinitatis). Which divinity? Deliberately vague.
  • Sol Invictus (the Unconquered Sun) stayed on his coins until about 320.
  • He kept the pagan title Pontifex Maximus (chief priest) all his life.
  • Baptised only on his deathbed, 337, by Eusebius of Nicomedia. Delaying baptism until near death was then common, so this does not prove insincerity.
  • Family violence: in 326 he had his son Crispus and his wife Fausta put to death.
Mission 4

Patronage of the church

  • Property and freedom: Christian property restored; freedom of worship agreed with Licinius (313; often called the "Edict of Milan", though the surviving text is Licinius' letter, Lactantius 48, Eusebius Church History 10.5).
  • Money and privileges: grants to clergy; clergy exempted from costly civic duties (313).
  • Buildings: the Lateran basilica in Rome (given to the bishop of Rome), St Peter's, the Church of the Holy Sepulchre in Jerusalem.
  • Law: bishops' courts could hear civil cases (318); Sunday made a day of rest (321: "the venerable day of the Sun"); no branding of convicts' faces (316); a ban on gladiator shows (325), little enforced.
  • A Christian capital: Constantinople founded (324), dedicated 330.
  • Bibles: he ordered fifty copies of the scriptures for its churches (Eusebius, Life 4.36).
Mission 4

From Africa to Nicaea

  • Donatists (North Africa): refused bishops who had handed over scriptures in the persecution. Constantine called the Council of Arles (314) and later used force against them, then gave up (321).
  • Licinius: after renewed tension (Licinius turned against Christians in the East), Constantine defeated him at Chrysopolis (324): sole emperor.
  • Arius: a dispute about whether the Son is fully God divided the eastern churches.
  • Constantine called the Council of Nicaea (325), attended and spoke; the bishops affirmed the Son "of one substance" (homoousios) with the Father.
  • He saw himself as a kind of "bishop of those outside" the church (Eusebius, Life 4.24).
Mission 4

Duality of motives

  • Sincere conversion: Constantine believed the Christian God gave him victory. Norman Baynes (1877–1961), Constantine the Great and the Christian Church (1931); Timothy Barnes (b. 1942), Constantine and Eusebius (1981).
  • Political calculation: a cool strategist who backed a growing, organised, empire-wide body. Jacob Burckhardt (1818–1897), The Age of Constantine the Great (1853).
  • Mixed or developing: a soldier's faith in a powerful God of victory, blending at first with sun worship and deepening over time.
  • His own letters often worry that God will punish the empire if the church is divided: religion as the safety of the state.
Quick check
?Which piece of evidence is most often used to argue that Constantine's early Christianity was mixed with sun worship?
Mission 4Evaluate

Faith or politics?

  • Claim: Constantine's support for Christianity was mainly political.
  • For: Christians were a minority in 312, but organised across the empire: useful allies.
  • For: Sol on coins, the title Pontifex Maximus, the vague Arch inscription, late baptism, and the deaths of Crispus and Fausta.
  • For: He used the church to unify the empire (Arles, Nicaea): one God, one emperor, one church.
  • Against: Backing a minority before a battle was a risk, not an obvious gain.
  • Against: His letters and laws are full of Christian conviction; he spent huge sums on churches; he educated his sons as Christians.
  • Against: Ancient people did not separate religion from politics: concern for God's favour on the state was religious.
  • Judgement criteria: Which sources are earliest and least biased? Can motives be known from actions? Is "sincere" and "political" a false choice?
Mission 4Evaluate

Conversion, and religion and state

  • Conversion (OAg): Is conversion a single moment or a process? Constantine's story is told as a moment (vision, victory) but looks like a journey (Sol, delayed baptism). Compare Paul (Acts 9) and Justin (see Mission 3).
  • What makes a conversion genuine: inner change, new behaviour, belonging (baptism)? On which criterion does Constantine pass or fail?
  • Religion and state (OAh): Was the "Constantinian shift" (the church's move from persecuted minority to imperial favour) a gain or a loss for the church?
  • Gain: freedom, safety, buildings, the end of persecution; Christian values in law (Sunday, limits on cruel punishments).
  • Loss: emperors interfering in doctrine; nominal members; the persecuted soon persecuting (Donatists, later pagans and heretics). Some Christians (e.g. Anabaptist traditions) see this as the church's "fall".
  • Today: established churches (the Church of England) vs separation of church and state (e.g. the USA): the same debate.
  • Judgement criteria: Does power corrupt the church's witness? Is a Christian state possible, or a contradiction?
Mission check

?A historian writes: "The sign on the shields is first described by a writer close to the court within three years of the battle; the sky vision appears only in a biography written a quarter of a century later." Which conclusion does this evidence best support?

The Milvian Bridge story grew over time, and how we judge Constantine depends on how we weigh the sources. Next in this unit: the wider Church and its leadership.

Mission 5

Mission 5: Should a church obey the government, guide it, or stand against it?

Make a guess: Should a church obey the government, guide it, or stand against it?

Mission 5

Three New Testament attitudes

  • Two spheres: "Give to Caesar the things that are Caesar's, and to God the things that are God's." (Mark 12:17)
  • Respect and prayer: authorities are "ordained by God" (Romans 13:1); pray "for kings and all who are in high places" (1 Timothy 2:2); "Honour the king." (1 Peter 2:17)
  • Limits: "We must obey God rather than men." (Acts 5:29)
  • Resistance: in Revelation 13 a persecuting empire is pictured as a beast making war on the saints.
  • Synoptic task: A2 4 students start from the Early Church, A2 5 students from the Celtic and post-Reformation church; both link to at least one other unit and to human experience.
Mission 5Read the source

Caesar and God

> "Give to Caesar the things that are Caesar's, and to God the things that are God's." (Mark 12:17, WEBBE)

> "Let every soul be in subjection to the higher authorities, for there is no authority except from God, and those who exist are ordained by God." (Romans 13:1, WEBBE)

Q1 Does Mark 12:17 say what belongs to Caesar?

Show answer

Not exactly: it accepts the state's claim to taxes but places God's claim above everything; much depends on interpretation.

Q2 Why is Romans 13:1 often read alongside Acts 5:29?

Show answer

Romans gives the state real authority; Acts sets its limit when it commands what God forbids.

Mission 5

The early church and Rome

  • Christians prayed for the emperor but would not sacrifice to him: refusal looked like disloyalty and led to persecution.
  • Apologists (Justin, Tertullian;) argued Christians were loyal, peaceful citizens.
  • Constantine (from 312) ended persecution and gave the church patronage, but also called councils and intervened in disputes (see Mission 4): the "Constantinian shift".
  • Theodosius I, Edict of Thessalonica (380): Nicene Christianity became the state's religion.
  • Ambrose, bishop of Milan, refused the emperor communion after the massacre at Thessalonica (390) until he did public penance: the church judging the ruler's morality.
Mission 5Read the source

Two cities, two powers

Augustine (354–430), City of God XIV.28 (413–426; Dods' translation):

> "Accordingly, two cities have been formed by two loves: the earthly by the love of self, even to the contempt of God; the heavenly by the love of God, even to the contempt of self."

  • Written after the sack of Rome (410): no earthly state, even a Christian one, is the City of God.
  • Pope Gelasius I (letter to Emperor Anastasius, 494), paraphrase: the world is ruled by two powers, the sacred authority of bishops and royal power; in spiritual matters the emperor should submit to the bishops.

Q1 What divides the two cities: territory or love?

Show answer

Love: of self or of God. Members of both live side by side in every state.

Q2 How does Gelasius go further than Augustine?

Show answer

He makes a claim about authority: spiritual power ranks above royal power in matters of faith.

Mission 5

Celtic church and kings

  • Patrick, Letter to Coroticus (5th century): condemns a British king's soldiers who killed and enslaved newly baptised converts, and declares them cut off from the church until they repent.
  • Colmcille: Adomnán says he ordained Áedán mac Gabráin king of Dál Riata (Life of Columba III.5) and records his part in the meeting of kings at Druim Cett.
  • Columbanus refused to bless Theuderic II's sons and was exiled (610).
  • Monasteries depended on royal patrons, yet abbots and saints acted as the conscience of kings.
  • Cáin Adomnáin (697): see the later screen.
Mission 5

After the Reformation

  • Royal supremacy (England 1534; Ireland 1537): the monarch heads the established church.
  • Peace of Augsburg (1555), later summed up as cuius regio, eius religio: the ruler decides the religion of the land.
  • Ireland: Penal Laws (from 1695) restricted Catholics' and, in some ways, Presbyterians' rights; Catholic Emancipation (1829).
  • Disestablishment: the Irish Church Act (1869, in force 1871) ended the Church of Ireland's status as state church.
  • Irish Constitution (1937), Article 44: the "special position" of the Catholic Church, removed by referendum in 1972.
  • Each step is a case study in how a church's link with the state affects freedom, belonging and conflict.
Mission 5Diversity

Models of religion and state

  • Theocracy / religious state: religious law or leaders hold state power (e.g. the Islamic Republic of Iran's 1979 constitution).
  • Established church: a national church linked to the state (Church of England: the monarch is Supreme Governor; bishops sit in the Lords).
  • Separation: no established church; free exercise of religion (USA, First Amendment, 1791; Jefferson's "wall of separation", 1802).
  • Strict secularism: religion kept out of state institutions (France, laïcité, law of 1905).
  • Christian traditions: Luther's two kingdoms; Calvin's cooperation of church and magistrate; Anabaptist separation from the state; Catholic teaching on cooperation with religious freedom (Dignitatis Humanae, 1965).
Quick check
?In which model does a national church keep a formal link with the state, with the head of state holding a title in the church?
Mission 5Evaluate

Should religion and state be closely linked?

  • Claim: The church is best served by a close relationship with the state.
  • For: freedom from persecution; Christian values in law (e.g. Constantine's Sunday law); a national church serves everyone (parishes, chaplaincies, ceremonies).
  • For: the church can act as the state's conscience from inside (Ambrose; bishops in the Lords).
  • Against: the state tends to control the church (emperors in councils; royal supremacy); the persecuted can become persecutors (penal laws).
  • Against: in a plural society, privilege for one faith may be unjust to others; Augustine: no earthly city is the City of God.
  • Judgement criteria: which model, in which society? Does closeness corrupt the church's witness or extend it? Freedom of religion for whom?
Mission 5

Lessons from history on moral issues

  • Slavery: Quakers petitioned Parliament against the slave trade (1783); evangelicals such as William Wilberforce led abolition (1807, 1833); yet other Christians defended slavery from scripture.
  • Nazi Germany: the Barmen Declaration (1934), largely drafted by Karl Barth, rejected the state's claim over the church; Dietrich Bonhoeffer was executed (1945). Many churches and Christians conformed.
  • Apartheid: the Dutch Reformed Church supported it for decades; Beyers Naudé and Desmond Tutu opposed it.
  • Ireland: inquiries such as the Ryan Report (2009) showed abuse in institutions run by religious orders and funded and inspected by the state: failure by church and state together.
Mission 5Evaluate

What lessons can be learned?

  • Claim: History shows that religion is a reliable moral guide in its dealings with the state.
  • For: believers led movements against slavery, Nazism and apartheid, often at great cost; Barmen and Ambrose show the church judging power.
  • Against: the same churches often backed injustice (slavery, apartheid) or kept silent (many German churches); close church–state ties in Ireland shielded abuse.
  • Lessons drawn: dangers of too close a bond with power; the value of a prophetic minority; the need for accountability to the law.
  • Judgement criteria: official churches or minorities within them? Judged by the standards of then or now? Religion as cause, or religion as cover for other interests?
Mission 5

Religion resolving conflict

  • Cáin Adomnáin (Law of Adomnán, Synod of Birr, 697): kings and churchmen agreed to protect women, children and clergy in war: an early law protecting non-combatants.
  • Peace of God (from the Synod of Charroux, 989) and Truce of God (1027): church councils limited private warfare in medieval France.
  • Mozambique: the Catholic Community of Sant'Egidio hosted talks leading to the Rome General Peace Accords (1992).
  • Northern Ireland: Fr Alec Reid (Redemptorist) and Rev. Harold Good (Methodist) witnessed IRA decommissioning (2005); church groups built trust across divides.
  • Liberia: Leymah Gbowee's interfaith women's movement (2003) pressed for peace; Nobel Peace Prize 2011.
Quick check
?Which example shows religious leaders making a law to protect non-combatants in war?
Mission 5Evaluate

Can religion resolve conflict?

  • Claim: Religion contributes more to resolving conflict than to causing it.
  • For: trusted, long-term presence on the ground; access to both sides (Sant'Egidio; Reid and Good); teachings on forgiveness and peace (Matthew 5:9).
  • For: historical laws limiting violence (Cáin Adomnáin, Peace of God).
  • Against: religion has marked the identities of opposing sides (Reformation wars; Northern Ireland; the Balkans); peace accords are made by politicians and states.
  • Against: some argue religious conflicts are really about land, power and identity, so religion is neither main cause nor main cure.
  • Judgement criteria: leaders or ordinary believers? Short-term mediation or long-term reconciliation? Religion as belief, institution or identity?
Mission check

?A government orders churches to preach that the nation's leader rules by divine right and must be obeyed without question. A synod refuses, declaring that Christ alone is Lord of the church. Which earlier stance does the synod's answer most closely follow?

Christian tradition gives the state real authority, but never the last word. That is why the relationship keeps being renegotiated.

Recap

The big ideas

Mission 1

  • Luke 22:17–20: Passover setting, new covenant, "given for you", "Do this in memory of me".
  • Catholic Mass: daily, priest, altar, transubstantiation, reservation; "source and summit".
  • Baptist Lord's Supper: less frequent, table, open, remembrance.

Mission 2

  • The Apostolic Fathers (about 90–150) wrote to churches about order, holiness, false teaching and persecution.
  • Ignatius, bishop of Antioch, wrote seven letters on his way to death in Rome under Trajan (about 107–117): one bishop with presbyters and deacons; against docetists and Judaisers; martyrdom as imitation of Christ.
  • Scholars debate whether he described or promoted episcopacy, and how to read his longing for martyrdom; his concerns remain live for leaders today.

Mission 3

  • Apologists answered charges of atheism, cannibalism and incest and asked for justice; Justin (c. 100–c. 165) wrote two Apologies and the Dialogue with Trypho.
  • Political (justice, loyalty), moral (changed lives), philosophical (the Logos and the seed of the Logos in all) and theological (Christ the Logos, proof from prophecy) arguments.
  • Evaluate success by audience and time-scale; apologetics serves believers, outsiders and public respect in different ways.

Mission 4

  • Constantine (c. 272–337) rose from the Tetrarchy to win the West at the Milvian Bridge (312) and the whole empire (324).
  • Lactantius (c. 314–315): a dream and a sign on shields. Eusebius (Life, after 337): a sky vision with "Conquer by this", a dream and the labarum.
  • Patronage (property, privileges, churches, Sunday, Nicaea) alongside Sol, Pontifex Maximus and late baptism: sincere, political or developing motives.

Mission 5

  • The New Testament holds respect for authority (Romans 13:1; 1 Peter 2:17) together with its limit (Acts 5:29; Mark 12:17); Augustine and Gelasius shaped later thought.
  • From Constantine, Ambrose, Patrick, Colmcille and Columbanus to royal supremacy, penal laws, disestablishment and modern models, church–state relations range from establishment to separation.
  • History teaches mixed lessons (slavery, Nazism, apartheid, abuse), but religion has also limited war and brokered peace (Cáin Adomnáin, Peace of God, Sant'Egidio, Northern Ireland).
